clue.text: Limitation on flowering plant's new life

parts.note: a rein is a check or restraint, so a limitation
the carnation is a popular flowering plant; the possessive adds no letter

explanation.surface: A botanist describes a restriction placed on a flower's fresh growth.
explanation.definitionFit: Being born again in another body after death is a fresh existence.

clue.text: Neat items put out in French cafe

indicators.note: put out suggests the letters are disturbed or displaced, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tidy articles are set outside a café in France.
explanation.definitionFit: An estaminet is a small French bar or bistro.

clue.text: Scandinavian river — what's under bridge crossing it?

indicators.note: the nose spans the river letter, which sits inside it

parts.note: the bridge of the nose is its top, so the nose lies beneath it

explanation.surface: A Nordic river, with a question about what lies beneath the bridge that spans it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bridge' suggests a structure over the river; it is the bridge of the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse describes the people and language of ancient Scandinavia.

clue.text: Distribute everything/nothing? Provide refreshments endlessly!

parts.note: all means everything
O is the figure zero, nothing

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to cater is to supply food and drink

explanation.surface: A host wonders whether to hand out everything or nothing, then urges catering without stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops R from CATER.
explanation.definitionFit: To allocate is to share out or assign portions.

clue.text: Form of massacre one day abroad

indicators.note: abroad means widely scattered or astray, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A killing spree takes place on a single day overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: A noyade was mass execution by drowning, used in the French Revolution at Nantes.
explanation.definitionFit: Mass execution by drowning, as at Nantes in 1793, is a kind of slaughter.

clue.text: Entertaining line could be produced by poet, right?

indicators.note: the result can be made from these letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet asks whether an amusing verse line might be his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'line' looks like a line of verse beside 'poet'; it is a cord for a circus act.
explanation.definitionFit: A high wire on which acrobats balance is a cord stretched to amuse an audience.

clue.text: Be involved in solemn promise — but have no time for sorcery

indicators.note: T is the abbreviation for time, and it is removed
the first piece goes inside the second

parts.note: an oath is a formal vow
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone joins in a vow but is too busy to dabble in magic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved in' gives OBEATH; 'have no time' then removes the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Obeah is a form of folk magic practised in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Basketball players get to catch high ball — wicked types!

indicators.note: the first word takes in the next piece, which goes inside it

parts.note: taken as written
a lob is a ball hit or thrown high into the air
rotters are nasty, unprincipled people

explanation.surface: Basketball stars must catch a lofted pass, unlike some villains.
explanation.walkthrough: The Harlem Globetrotters are a famous US exhibition basketball team.
explanation.definitionFit: The Harlem Globetrotters are a touring exhibition basketball team.

clue.text: Teach prisoner somehow to become a dancer

indicators.note: by some unspecified means, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An inmate is taught to become a dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: Terpsichore is the Greek Muse of dance; the word is used as a noun for a dancer.
explanation.definitionFit: From the Muse of dance, the word names a performer of dancing.

clue.text: American measure put to friendly country precisely

parts.note: LITER is the American spelling of the metric unit of volume
an ally is a nation on friendly terms with another

explanation.surface: A US unit of measurement is offered to a nation on good terms, exactly.
explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling is LITRE; 'American' tells you to use the US form, which ends -ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an intensifier, the adverb means exactly or to the letter.

clue.text: Birds we see gliding — just some swirling around

indicators.note: spinning round means the run found in the clue is read backwards
only some of the letters in the words that follow are used, a run inside them

explanation.surface: Watching birds in flight, only a few of them are circling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just some' picks ESEEG from 'wE SEE Gliding', and 'swirling around' turns it back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Large waterfowl such as greylags are a kind of bird.

clue.text: Dessert was a disaster, not finished

indicators.note: the word is left without its ending, so its final letter goes

parts.note: to have bombed is slang for having flopped or failed badly

explanation.surface: A cook laments that a pudding flopped and was left half-made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finished' cuts the last letter, D, from BOMBED.
explanation.definitionFit: A bombe is a moulded frozen pudding, often ice cream, shaped like a dome.

clue.text: In position of one being trained, Ted is chap to be licked into shape

indicators.note: licking something into shape means reorganising it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A recruit named Ted is a fellow who must be knocked into shape during training.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal 'to be licked into shape' fits the surface's picture of a raw trainee being disciplined.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a trainee in the forces or police, and the -ship suffix makes it the status held.

clue.text: Perseverance of number joining a big community

parts.note: ten is a number
a city is a large urban community

explanation.surface: Persistence shown by a group of people who join a big town.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenacity is dogged determination, the quality of holding on and not giving up.

clue.text: Happy having got about in several countries

indicators.note: the first word goes round the next, holding it inside

parts.note: content means satisfied, happy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller is pleased to have toured several nations.
explanation.definitionFit: A continent is a large landmass containing many nations.

clue.text: One shows evidence of limited growth in Japan?

definitions.text: One shows evidence of limited growth in Japan?

parts.words: One shows evidence of limited growth in Japan?
parts.note: sounds like a remark on a stalled Japanese economy, but describes a deliberately dwarfed tree grown in a pot, a Japanese art

explanation.surface: An economist points to a sign of sluggish growth in the Japanese economy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limited growth' suggests economics; it is really a miniature tree kept small by pruning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of growing miniature trees in containers keeps them tiny by root and branch pruning.

clue.text: Vehicles don't observe proper discipline on motorway?

definitions.meaning: aircraft fitted with runners for landing on snow

definitions.text: don't observe proper discipline on motorway?
definitions.meaning: to jump from one traffic lane to another, ignoring lane discipline

explanation.surface: Drivers ignore lane discipline on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vehicles' looks like cars on the road; it means aircraft equipped with skis.
explanation.definitionFit: Aircraft with skis are flying machines, and skipping lanes is ignoring proper road lanes.

clue.text: One has upset a woman, a Spanish one

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned over means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: one's, a contraction of one has, gives these letters
Rita is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman has knocked over another woman, a Spanish lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns ONES into SENO. 'one' at the end stands for 'woman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Señorita is the Spanish title for a young or unmarried lady.

clue.text: Old church used for housing brown chemical

indicators.note: the church letters hold the brown letters inside them

parts.note: CE stands for Church of England
tan is a light brown colour

explanation.surface: A disused old church now serves as a store for a brown substance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'housing' looks like shelter for people in the old church; it is the container signal, and CE (Church of England) is the usual crossword abbreviation for church.
explanation.definitionFit: Octane is a hydrocarbon compound found in petrol, hence a chemical.

clue.text: "French sea" by female author

parts.note: mer is the French word for sea
Edith is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A book titled 'French Sea' written by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith was a Victorian English novelist and poet.
explanation.definitionFit: George Meredith wrote The Egoist and other Victorian novels, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Mum needs doctor when these snakes bite dangerously

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
MB is a medical degree, Bachelor of Medicine
as can mean when, at the time that

explanation.surface: A mother must see a doctor when bitten by venomous snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the description of the snakes, whose venomous bite sends victims to a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Mambas are highly venomous African snakes whose bite can kill.

clue.text: Staged work features kid at home being naughty

indicators.note: a child misbehaving is unruly, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A theatre piece shows a child at home misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera is a piece performed on stage.

clue.text: Duck shows hesitation eating fish

indicators.note: the first piece takes the second inside it

parts.note: er is the sound of hesitating
the ide is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A duck pauses while it eats a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck prized for its down.

clue.text: Secretary who fusses with her nails?

definitions.text: Secretary who fusses with her nails?

parts.words: Secretary who fusses with her nails?
parts.note: an office worker who files papers away, and also someone who smooths fingernails with an emery board

explanation.surface: An office secretary spends her time on a manicure.
explanation.walkthrough: One who files is both a clerk storing documents and someone shaping nails with a nail file.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerk who puts documents into files does the same verb as someone shaping nails with an emery board.

clue.text: Lent perhaps broken by start of Easter celebration

indicators.note: a piece placed inside breaks the word open

parts.note: Lent is an example of a period of fasting

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: only its first letter is used; that the clue's 'of Easter' also happens to spell the answer forwards is a coincidence, not the setter's device

explanation.surface: The Lenten fast ends with the arrival of Easter festivities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks Lent as an example of a fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A feast is a festive meal or religious festival.

clue.text: There's little good in bad-mannered Dickensian character

indicators.note: the short form for good goes inside the word for impolite

parts.note: rude means impolite
G is the short form of good

explanation.surface: A Dickens figure has scarcely any goodness despite his rough manners.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnaby Rudge is the title character of a Dickens novel. 'little' signals the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnaby Rudge is the hero of the Dickens novel named after him.

clue.text: Woman of the country

parts.note: looks like a rural woman, but means the female figure personifying a nation, shown with helmet, shield and trident

explanation.surface: A countrywoman from the rural shires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of the country' suggests rustic life; the woman stands for Great Britain itself, as on old British coins.
explanation.definitionFit: The helmeted female figure on British coinage is the personification of the nation.

clue.text: Form of religion in which characters could get smitten with pastor

indicators.note: the letters could be made into another word, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A faith in which believers might fall for their minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could get' signals a rearrangement of SMITTEN and PASTOR together; 'with' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: The faith of the Reformed churches that broke from Rome is a branch of Christianity.
